newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - New Hungary insurance law fails to open market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New Hungary insurance law fails to open market.

text.p: A new Hungarian insurance law designed partly to increase competition has so far failed to open the market, regulators and insurance industry sources say.

The law, in effect since January 1, abolished a capital requirement of 1 billion forints ($6.30 million) for setting up an insurance company, three times the European Union average, and halved the maximum capital to 450 million forints.
Despite this, only two companies, Hermes, which was recently bought by Allianz, and Zurich, have appeared on the Hungarian market since the law was changed, and both had been anticipated beforehand.

"Everybody was expecting that just because the required capital has been reduced significantly there would be a lot of newcomers on the market," said Barnabas Trunko, secretary general of the Assocation of Hungarian Insurance Companies.
"But only two new companies have been formed in the last 10 months and both of them had been anticipated by the experts."
SEVERAL FACTORS TO BLAME

Industry and regulatory sources cite several factors for the slow uptake, including inflation averaging more than 20 percent a year and the presence already in Hungary of some of the world's biggest insurers, including Allianz, EA Generali AG, Nationale Nederlanden and Aegon NV.
There is also a perception that the Hungarian market will not grow as fast as some others in eastern and central Europe.
"If you look at Hungary, I think it's not the biggest east European market," said Andras Juhos, deputy general manager of AB-Aegon, the leader in the Hungarian life insurance market.
Juhos added that the economy was a constraint on growth.

"If you are relatively poor then there is a place for every forint that you earn," he said. "You have to buy food, you have to buy clothes, you may have to buy a car and only what remains then goes on insurance or something like that."

Despite such concerns, however, industry experts think the law is a major change for the better and should go a long way towards improving the image in Hungary of insurance, which has a somewhat clouded reputation because of the legacy of a nationwide group insurance plan adopted in communist times.
That policy, known as the CSEB and initiated in the 1960s, promised comprehensive insurance at rock-bottom prices, but premiums and benefits were fixed before inflation skyrocketed.

With premiums starting as low as the equivalent of 10 U.S. cents a month, millions of Hungarians signed up for policies offering death, hospital, disability, unemployment and other benefits at rates almost everyone could afford.

"I think it was the biggest group life insurance in the world," said Juhos, whose company ended up with millions of the policies when the state insurance industry was broken up a decade ago and its business parcelled out.

Inflation has made the top CSEB premium today, 150 forints, the equivalent of about $1. Benefits also have eroded but clients, although disappointed with payouts which 15 years ago would have been significant, keep the policies because the premiums are so low it isn't worth dropping out, Juhos said.

"This product is clearly a catastrophe," he said. "Its claim frequency is one claim in every fourth year...and claim settlement is not that cheap. So you can see that the inflation in this product was a catastrophe for my company which really inherited the portfolio."
INDUSTRY HAS GENERALLY TURNED THE CORNER

That said, the Hungarian insurance industry generally has turned the corner from years of unprofitability, despite overall stagnation of the economy, where GDP growth has been two percent or less for the last two years.

Life insurance companies had premium income of 33.98 billion forints in 1995, up from 23.43 billion in 1994, while non-life companies had premium income of 82.87 billion forints in 1995 versus 69.39 billion forints in 1994, according to insurance association statistics.

"Last year (1995) was the first healthy year...after years of consolidation," said Sandor Dogei, chief economist at Hungary's State Insurance Supervising Authority. "It was also the first year when four Hungarian companies showed a little profit."
Dogei said the new law incorporates a host of other changes which should benefit the industry and the insured.
Previously, insurance companies wanting to set up in Hungary had to get a licence from the government. Now all that is needed is a licence from the supervising authority.
"The act defines what we have to see...We can't make any other requirements," Dogei said. "There is a list and if you meet those requirements we have to give permission."
The new law also sets solvency margins which, while they may be onerous for the companies, provide an extra measure of safety for policy-holders, Dogei said.
"The EU uses this too and every company has to have some free capital above their needs," he said.

For AB-Aegon, the solvency margin means the money in the business has risen from about one billion forints to more than nine billion -- "which means that shareholders expect returns on that...and I have to be more profitable," Juhos said.

Juhos also said the government policy of offering tax breaks of 50 percent on money wage earners pump into non-profit pension funds, but only 20 percent for funds invested in life insurance, put insurance companies at a disadvantage for that segment of the market.

But Hungarians generally carry fairly low levels of insurance compared with the rest of the developed world, leaving room for growth. In Britain, for example, some five percent of GDP goes into life insurance or pension savings while the level in Hungary is 0.6 percent, industry sources say.

"It's a good law," said Trunko. "It took years to make it and it has been made in accordance with European standards so that when we become members of the EU it can be used 100 percent." ($1=158.79 Forint)
